name: Mexenone

angle.text: Mexenone is an older benzophenone sunscreen filter, used to keep UV from damaging skin and so to slow sun-driven wrinkling and uneven tone. It is known more from dermatology allergy clinics than from current skincare routines, and its protective role is established chemistry rather than appearance trials.

summary: Old benzophenone sunscreen filter (benzophenone-10) known mostly as a contact and photoallergen in dermatology clinics.
note: Reported as a leading sunscreen allergen in 1980s-90s patch-test series.
currentQuick:
Mexenone is a benzophenone-type UV filter once used in sunscreens, also called benzophenone-10. It is related to oxybenzone.
Much of what is published about it concerns allergic reactions, not skin-protection performance.
How it works: Like other benzophenones it absorbs ultraviolet light through its aromatic ketone structure. Published sources reviewed here do not give its specific absorption range.
Risks and caveats: Dermatology patch-test series reported mexenone among the most frequent sunscreen allergens, with roughly 5 to 7.5% of tested patients reacting to sunscreens overall. Its current regulatory status was not documented in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Mexenone (benzophenone-10, trade name Uvistat) is a benzophenone-derived sunscreening agent with the chemical name (2-hydroxy-4-methoxyphenyl)(4-methylphenyl)methanone (C15H14O3). It is chemically related to oxybenzone (benzophenone-3).
It is mainly known in the medical literature as a contact and photocontact allergen. Patch-test series from clinics in the 1980s and 1990s repeatedly reported mexenone as one of the most frequent sunscreen sensitisers. Little else about its performance as a cosmetic ingredient is documented in the sources reviewed.

name: Gadusol

angle.text: Gadusol is a natural UV-absorbing molecule from fish roe that researchers have explored as a bio-derived sunscreen ingredient. People interested in natural photoprotection cite it as a way to limit sun-driven skin aging; the evidence is lab and computational work, with no human appearance trials.

summary: Natural fish-roe UV absorber studied as a bio-derived sunscreen molecule; lab and computational work only, no human trials.
note: Not an established cosmetic ingredient; no human studies found.
currentQuick:
Gadusol is a small molecule that fish eggs and some other animals carry to absorb sunlight. It is related to the mycosporine-like amino acids made by algae and corals.
Researchers have proposed it as a natural sunscreen ingredient and have engineered microbes to produce it.
How it works: Its conjugated ring structure absorbs UV radiation, and it also has antioxidant activity measured in fish-roe extracts.
Risks and caveats: No human safety or efficacy studies were found. It is not an established commercial sunscreen filter.
deepLead:
Gadusol is a small natural UV-absorbing compound (C8H12O6), a substituted cyclohexenone, found in the eggs of fish and in some other vertebrates and invertebrates. It was isolated from cod roe, where it occurs at about 4 g per kg dry weight, and its structure was confirmed by synthesis in 1981. It is related to the mycosporine-like amino acids that organisms in high-sunlight environments use as natural sunscreens.
Because it absorbs UV and has antioxidant properties, gadusol has been proposed as a sunscreen or cosmetic ingredient and has been studied computationally, photophysically and in bioengineered production systems. No human trials of gadusol as a topical product were found.

name: Umbelliferone

angle.text: Umbelliferone is a plant coumarin that absorbs UV light and is listed as a sunscreen agent, so it is mentioned as a way to limit sun damage that ages skin. Support for its use on skin comes from lab chemistry and animal work rather than human appearance studies.

summary: Plant coumarin that absorbs UVB/short UVA and is listed as a sunscreen agent; actual evidence is lab chemistry and animal work.
note: No human studies as a sunscreen; Wikipedia flags weak sourcing on some uses.
currentQuick:
Umbelliferone is a natural coumarin found in carrots, coriander, angelica and hydrangea. It absorbs ultraviolet light and glows blue, which is why it appears as a sunscreen agent and a fluorescent dye.
Research on it is mostly laboratory and animal work on antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects.
How it works: The coumarin ring absorbs UV around 300 to 325 nm. In cell and animal studies it is reported to act on the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway.
Risks and caveats: No human safety or efficacy trials as a sunscreen were found. Its absorption shifts in alkaline conditions, and related furanocoumarins such as psoralen are distinct compounds.
deepLead:
Umbelliferone (7-hydroxycoumarin, C9H6O3) is a natural coumarin found in plants of the carrot family (Apiaceae) such as carrot, coriander and garden angelica, and in hydrangea and asafoetida. It absorbs UV light strongly at about 300 to 325 nm and fluoresces blue, and is listed on Wikipedia as having been used as a sunscreen agent as well as an optical brightener and a fluorescent indicator.
Most published work concerns its use as a fluorescent probe, its metabolism, and animal and laboratory research on antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. No human trials of umbelliferone as a sunscreen or appearance product were found.

name: Padimate A

angle.text: Padimate A is a PABA-ester sunscreen filter related to the better-known padimate O, and it appears in discussions of historical sunscreen ingredients. Its role is UV protection that helps keep skin from sun-driven aging; it has little modern research and was never US-approved.

summary: Obscure PABA-ester sunscreen filter, withdrawn in Europe in 1989 and never US-approved; essentially no modern research on it.
note: Reported withdrawn in Europe (1989) and not approved in the US.
currentQuick:
Padimate A is a PABA-derived UV filter, a close relative of padimate O. It saw limited use in sunscreens but is not a current mainstream ingredient.
Very little padimate A-specific research is available.
How it works: Like other PABA esters it absorbs UVB through its aminobenzoate structure.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia reports it was withdrawn in Europe in 1989 and never approved in the US, and that padimates raised photochemical safety questions in cell studies. No clinical studies were found.
deepLead:
Padimate A (isoamyl p-dimethylaminobenzoate, Escalol 506) is a PABA-ester UV filter, a dimethylated ester of 4-aminobenzoic acid. It is chemically related to padimate O (octyl dimethyl PABA), a much more widely studied sunscreen ingredient. Wikipedia states it was withdrawn in Europe in 1989 and was never approved for use in sunscreens in the US.
Published concerns about the padimate class involve photochemistry: Wikipedia reports that padimate A and padimate O resemble an industrial free-radical generator and increased the lethal effects of UV on cells in cited studies. Little padimate A-specific research was found, and no clinical studies exist in the sources reviewed.

name: Benzophenone-9

angle.text: Benzophenone-9 is a water-soluble UV-absorbing compound that appears on lists of sunscreen ingredients, where the aim is limiting sun damage that ages skin. Published material is mostly environmental and analytical chemistry rather than studies of cosmetic benefit.

summary: A water-soluble benzophenone UV filter with almost no published human data; mostly appears in environmental chemistry papers.
note: Very little published research on cosmetic use.
currentQuick:
Benzophenone-9 is a water-soluble ultraviolet-absorbing chemical listed among benzophenone sunscreen filters.
Published work on it is thin: a few environmental and laboratory studies, and no human trials of its skin-protective effect.
How it works: Like other benzophenones, it absorbs ultraviolet light. A lab study found it blocked UV-driven bacterial killing in water.
Risks and caveats: A 2022 study did not detect it in urine or blood samples from young adults. Benzophenone filters as a group have been described as endocrine-disrupting chemicals in the literature; BP-9 itself has little safety data in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Benzophenone-9 (BP-9) is a water-soluble benzophenone-type ultraviolet-absorbing compound that appears in lists of sunscreen and UV-filter ingredients. Published material on it is sparse and consists mostly of environmental and analytical chemistry rather than studies of cosmetic benefit.
In a 2022 study of 196 paired urine and blood samples from young adults in South China, benzophenone-7 and benzophenone-9 were not detected in any sample, while other benzophenone-type filters were widely found. A 2017 laboratory study examined how BP-9 and benzophenone-4 break down under a UV/hydrogen peroxide water-treatment process, identifying 17 degradation products for BP-9.

name: HAA299

angle.text: HAA299 is an experimental sunscreen filter designed to cover long-wave UVA-1 and the edge of visible light, wavelengths linked to skin aging and pigmentation. It has a small early study and an EU safety-committee opinion, with no long-term appearance trials.

summary: An experimental UVA-1/visible-edge sunscreen filter with a small early study and an EU safety-committee opinion.
note: Experimental; not established as a marketed consumer ingredient in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
HAA299 is an experimental organic sunscreen filter aimed at long-wave UVA and the violet edge of visible light.
One small volunteer study reported protection against light-induced pigmentation at 385 and 405 nm, and the EU's SCCS reviewed a nano form in 2021.
How it works: It absorbs light at the boundary between ultraviolet and visible wavelengths, which can trigger skin pigmentation through oxidative stress.
Risks and caveats: Safety was assessed by the SCCS for the nano form; details are in the full opinion. Evidence in people is limited to a single small pigmentation study.
deepLead:
HAA299, with the INCI name bis-(diethylaminohydroxybenzoyl benzoyl) piperazine, is an experimental organic UV filter designed to absorb long-wave UVA (UVA-1) and the violet edge of visible light. The EU's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) issued a scientific opinion on a nano form of HAA299 in 2021, describing it as a UV filter intended for sunscreen products to protect skin against UVA-1 rays.
A 2022 study reported that a visible-light-absorbing filter of this type offered protection against pigmentation induced by wavelengths at the boundary of ultraviolet and visible light.

name: Acitretin

angle.text: Acitretin is a prescription oral retinoid used for severe psoriasis and keratinisation disorders, so it is discussed in skin-appearance circles as a clinical retinoid option. Its evidence is in those medical conditions; use for cosmetic skin goals is off the label and not studied.

summary: A prescription oral retinoid for severe psoriasis and keratinisation disorders, with strict pregnancy-prevention rules.
note: Highly teratogenic; contraception required during and for about three years after treatment.
currentQuick:
Acitretin is an oral vitamin A-derived drug prescribed for severe psoriasis and certain disorders where skin thickens and scales abnormally.
It is a treatment for skin disease, not an established cosmetic; studies of purely cosmetic use were not found.
How it works: It binds nuclear retinoid receptors and shifts gene activity so skin cells mature normally and over-multiply less. Its half-life is about two days.
Risks and caveats: Documented risks include severe birth defects, dry skin and lips, hair loss, raised blood fats and rare liver problems. It is prescription-only, with pregnancy prevention required for about three years after use.
deepLead:
Acitretin is an oral second-generation retinoid used for severe psoriasis that has not responded to other treatments, and off-label for several disorders of keratinisation. It is the active metabolite of etretinate and is sold under brand names including Soriatane and Neotigason. It is a prescription-only drug in the US, UK, Canada and Australia.
Its relevance to appearance is as a treatment for visible skin disease rather than as a cosmetic. Its best-known risk is severe teratogenicity: the labelling and reviews require strict pregnancy prevention during treatment and for years afterwards. Common side effects resemble vitamin A excess, including dry skin and lips and hair loss.

name: Etretinate

angle.text: Etretinate is a withdrawn oral retinoid once prescribed for severe psoriasis, mentioned in skin forums as the predecessor of acitretin. Its effect on visible skin was studied in psoriasis and keratinisation disorders; cosmetic use is untested.

summary: A withdrawn oral retinoid for severe psoriasis, replaced by acitretin because it lingered in the body for years.
note: Withdrawn in the US and Canada; teratogenic risk persists for years after use.
currentQuick:
Etretinate was an oral vitamin A-derived drug for severe psoriasis, approved in the US in 1986 and withdrawn in the late 1990s.
It treated skin disease and was not a cosmetic; it has been replaced by acitretin.
How it works: It converts to acitretin and binds retinoid receptors to normalise skin-cell maturation. It is stored in body fat and has a half-life of about 120 days.
Risks and caveats: Because it persists for years, birth-defect risk lasts long after treatment. Other effects include dry skin and lips and bone or joint pain. It is no longer sold in the US or Canada.
deepLead:
Etretinate (brand names Tegison, Tigason) is a second-generation oral retinoid developed by Hoffmann-La Roche for severe psoriasis and related keratinisation disorders. The US FDA approved it in 1986, and Roche voluntarily withdrew it from the Canadian market in 1996 and the US market in 1998 because of its very long elimination half-life and teratogenic potential. Wikipedia lists it as still marketed in Japan.
Its successor is acitretin, the free acid and an active metabolite, which has a much shorter half-life. Etretinate is a treatment for skin disease rather than a cosmetic agent.

name: Alitretinoin

angle.text: Alitretinoin (9-cis-retinoic acid) is a prescription retinoid used orally for severe chronic hand eczema and as a gel for Kaposi's sarcoma lesions. It comes up in skin discussions as a retinoid with visible skin effects, supported by trials in those conditions rather than cosmetic use.

summary: A prescription retinoid for severe chronic hand eczema (oral) and Kaposi's sarcoma lesions (gel), not a cosmetic.
note: Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication for oral use.
currentQuick:
Alitretinoin is a form of retinoic acid used as a prescription capsule for severe long-term hand eczema and as a gel for Kaposi's sarcoma skin lesions.
It treats skin disease; no source reviewed tested it for cosmetic purposes.
How it works: It activates both main families of retinoid receptors, changing gene activity that controls skin-cell growth and immune signalling.
Risks and caveats: Oral use can cause headache, raised blood lipids and dry skin and lips, and is contraindicated in pregnancy. The gel commonly causes local rash and pain.
deepLead:
Alitretinoin (9-cis-retinoic acid) is a naturally occurring retinoid that activates both retinoic acid receptors and retinoid X receptors. It is marketed as a topical gel (Panretin) for skin lesions of AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma and as oral capsules (Toctino) for severe chronic hand eczema unresponsive to potent topical corticosteroids. It was developed by Ligand Pharmaceuticals.
It is a prescription medicine for skin disease; no source examined it as a cosmetic. Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication for oral use, and common effects include headache and raised blood lipids.

name: Seletinoid G

angle.text: Seletinoid G is a lab-designed retinoid intended as a topical anti-aging ingredient that irritates less than tretinoin. It is aimed at aged and photoaged skin; the evidence is a tiny short human study plus skin-model work.

summary: A Korean lab-designed retinoid for aging skin, tested only in a tiny short study and skin models.
note: Not an approved drug; no patient trials of visible anti-aging effect found.
currentQuick:
Seletinoid G is an experimental retinoid designed on a computer to treat aged skin with less irritation than tretinoin.
Human data are limited to a 23-person, four-day experiment on the buttocks and lab skin-model work; no patient trials are known.
How it works: As a retinoid it is intended to act on skin cells to influence extracellular matrix proteins such as collagen; the 2005 study measured these proteins, and a 2020 study examined barrier function and wound healing in skin models.
Risks and caveats: Its stated aim was lower irritation than tretinoin, based on the small 2005 comparison. It has no approved status and no long-term safety data were found.
deepLead:
Seletinoid G is an experimental synthetic retinoid that was designed with computer-aided molecular modeling by Korean researchers as a topical anti-aging ingredient intended to cause less skin irritation than all-trans retinoic acid (tretinoin). Published work on it concerns aged and photoaged skin, with a related line of laboratory work on skin barrier repair.
The published human evidence is limited to a small short-term in vivo experiment in 23 volunteers using occlusive application on the buttocks, reported in 2005, and to laboratory work in reconstructed human skin models in 2020. No large randomized trials of seletinoid G for wrinkles or acne have been identified, and it is not an approved drug. Discussion of it in looksmaxxing communities was not found in the available sources.

name: Motretinide

angle.text: Motretinide is an older topical retinoid that was used for acne and compared with benzoyl peroxide in a 1984 trial. It is mentioned mainly as a historical acne retinoid, with little modern literature.

summary: A largely historical topical acne retinoid with a 1984 trial against benzoyl peroxide and little modern literature.
note: Not in common use; retinoids as a class carry teratogenicity concerns.
currentQuick:
Motretinide is an older topical retinoid that was used for acne. Wikipedia describes it as an aromatic analogue of retinoic acid and a stub-level entry.
Most published work dates from the 1980s, including one comparison with benzoyl peroxide.
How it works: Like other retinoids it acts through nuclear retinoid receptors in skin cells, affecting keratinization; animal assays from the 1980s measured this antikeratinizing effect.
Risks and caveats: Aromatic retinoids as a class have teratogenic potential, and motretinide was included in teratogenicity screening work. Current regulatory and marketing status is not stated in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Motretinide is an aromatic retinoid, an analogue of retinoic acid, classed as a topical anti-acne agent (ATC code D10AD05). It has been described as a retinoid once used on the skin for acne; it is not among the retinoids in common use today.
The published evidence is mostly from the 1980s: a comparison against benzoyl peroxide in acne vulgaris, animal assays of retinoid activity, and teratogenicity testing alongside other retinoids. Discussion of it in looksmaxxing communities was not found in the available sources.

name: Tazarotenic acid

angle.text: Tazarotenic acid is the active form that prescription tazarotene converts into on the skin, and tazarotene is promoted by some users as a strong anti-aging retinoid. Photoaging evidence exists for tazarotene itself; the metabolite alone is not sold or studied for looks.

summary: The active acid form of prescription tazarotene; evidence exists for the parent retinoid's photoaging effect, not for the metabolite alone.
note: Parent drug is contraindicated in pregnancy; irritation is common.
currentQuick:
Tazarotenic acid is what the body makes from tazarotene, a prescription topical retinoid used for acne, psoriasis and photodamage. It is not sold on its own.
A 12-month trial of tazarotene cream showed improvement in wrinkles and pigmentation versus vehicle. No studies have tested the acid alone.
How it works: Skin and blood esterases convert tazarotene to tazarotenic acid, which binds retinoic acid receptors, selectively RAR-beta and RAR-gamma, altering keratinocyte growth and differentiation.
Risks and caveats: Irritation is the most common effect of the parent drug. It is contraindicated in pregnancy. Prescription-only in the US.
deepLead:
Tazarotenic acid is the active metabolite of tazarotene, a prescription topical retinoid. Tazarotene is a prodrug: after it is applied to the skin, esterase enzymes rapidly remove its ethyl ester group, producing the free acid that binds retinoic acid receptors . It is not sold as a separate product; people encounter it through tazarotene (brands such as Tazorac, Arazlo and Fabior) .
Tazarotenic acid binds retinoic acid receptors (RARs) but not retinoid X receptors, and in laboratory assays it is selective for the RAR-beta and RAR-gamma subtypes . Tazarotene is approved in the United States for acne, plaque psoriasis and, in some formulations, photodamage, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy .
In forum discussion, tazarotene is sometimes described as a stronger alternative to tretinoin for skin texture and anti-aging. No published study has tested tazarotenic acid as a stand-alone cosmetic ingredient; the human evidence concerns the parent drug.

name: Oleyl adapalenate

angle.text: Oleyl adapalenate (Adapinoid) is a cosmetic retinoid pro-drug of adapalene, positioned for photoaging with better tolerability than retinol. Evidence for that use is one small 2024 trial suggesting improved wrinkles compared with retinol.

summary: A newer adapalene-ester cosmetic retinoid with one small 2024 trial suggesting better wrinkle results and tolerability than retinol.
note: Evidence rests on one 48-person, 12-week trial.
currentQuick:
Oleyl adapalenate is a cosmetic ingredient described as a pro-drug of the acne and photoaging retinoid adapalene.
A single 12-week trial of 48 people found it improved wrinkles more than retinol and was better tolerated.
How it works: It is described as a pro-drug that releases adapalene, a retinoid, in the skin.
Risks and caveats: Little safety research exists beyond the one trial, which reported better tolerability than retinol.
deepLead:
Oleyl adapalenate (marketed as Adapinoid) is described in the literature as a third-generation retinoid and a pro-drug of adapalene, formed by joining adapalene to an oleyl group . It is used in cosmetic skincare creams aimed at photoaging, positioned as a retinoid with better tolerability.
Published evidence is limited to a small number of studies. A 2024 randomized, double-blind, 12-week trial of 48 people compared 0.5% oleyl adapalenate cream with 0.5% retinol cream and reported greater wrinkle improvement with oleyl adapalenate and better tolerability .

name: Liarozole

angle.text: Liarozole is an investigational drug that raises the skin's own retinoic acid levels, and it was tested orally in psoriasis and ichthyosis. People interested in retinoid-style skin renewal cite it as a mechanism; cosmetic use has no evidence.

summary: An older oral retinoic-acid blocker tested in psoriasis and ichthyosis, with no cosmetic evidence.
note: Investigational; not approved for any use.
currentQuick:
Liarozole is an investigational oral drug that raises the body's own retinoic acid levels by blocking its breakdown.
It was tested in psoriasis, ichthyosis and prostate cancer, not for cosmetic skin ageing.
How it works: It inhibits CYP26 enzymes that degrade retinoic acid, and also inhibits aromatase and CYP17A1.
Risks and caveats: In a small psoriasis trial, itching, cheilitis and dry skin were most common. It is not approved.
deepLead:
Liarozole is an investigational imidazole-type drug classed as a retinoic acid metabolism blocking agent (RAMBA). It inhibits the cytochrome P450 enzyme that breaks down all-trans-retinoic acid, raising retinoic acid levels in tissues, and it also inhibits aromatase and CYP17A1 . It was studied orally for psoriasis, ichthyosis and prostate cancer .
It is not an approved cosmetic and its interest to appearance communities is indirect, as a forerunner of newer retinoic acid blockers such as talarozole. Published trials concern skin disorders, not cosmetic skin ageing.

name: Talarozole

angle.text: Talarozole is an investigational retinoic-acid blocker developed for acne and psoriasis, raising retinoid signalling without supplying a retinoid. Development for skin use was discontinued, and cosmetic use is untested.

summary: An investigational retinoic-acid blocker shelved for acne and psoriasis, now explored for osteoarthritis; no cosmetic evidence.
note: Not approved; early-phase data only.
currentQuick:
Talarozole is an investigational drug that raises retinoic acid levels in tissue by blocking its breakdown. It was tested for acne and psoriasis, and skin development is reported discontinued.
No studies cover cosmetic use.
How it works: It inhibits CYP26A1 and CYP26B1, the enzymes that clear all-trans-retinoic acid.
Risks and caveats: A small volunteer study found low irritation with topical use. It is not approved and long-term data are lacking.
deepLead:
Talarozole (formerly R115866; planned trade name Rambazole) is an investigational retinoic acid metabolism blocking agent (RAMBA). It inhibits the CYP26 enzymes, mainly CYP26A1 and CYP26B1, that break down all-trans-retinoic acid, so it raises retinoic acid signaling without supplying a retinoid . It was developed for acne, psoriasis and other keratinization disorders, and development for those skin uses is reported as discontinued .
Human data are early-phase. A small phase I study of topical talarozole on healthy volunteers found gene-expression changes consistent with increased retinoic acid signaling and little irritation . More recently it has attracted attention in osteoarthritis research . It is not approved anywhere and has no established cosmetic use.

name: Retinyl esters

chain: Convert to retinol then retinoic acid
angle.text: Retinyl esters such as palmitate, acetate and propionate are used in creams as milder, more stable alternatives to retinol and tretinoin for anti-aging. They are promoted for smoother texture and fewer lines; skin outcome evidence is thin.

summary: Vitamin A's storage esters, used in creams as gentler retinol alternatives; skin evidence is thin.
note: Sunscreen-use safety debated; excess vitamin A is toxic.
currentQuick:
Retinyl esters are the form in which the body stores vitamin A, also used in cosmetics as milder retinoid ingredients.
No trials in the sources reviewed tested them for appearance.
How it works: In skin they are described as converting to retinol and then retinoic acid, though conversion is said to be inefficient.
Risks and caveats: Excess preformed vitamin A causes hypervitaminosis A. Sunscreen use of retinyl palmitate prompted a mouse-study debate.
deepLead:
Retinyl esters are fatty-acid esters of retinol (vitamin A), the main form in which the body stores vitamin A, chiefly as retinyl palmitate in the liver . In cosmetics, retinyl palmitate, acetate and propionate are used as milder, more stable alternatives to retinol and tretinoin .
In skin, esters are described as converting to retinol and then to retinoic acid, though Wikipedia states neither absorption nor conversion is very efficient . No trials of retinyl esters for cosmetic appearance were found in the sources reviewed.

name: Retinyl acetate

angle.text: Retinyl acetate is a stable vitamin A ester that appears in some anti-aging skincare as a gentler retinol alternative. Users apply it for smoother, younger-looking skin; no appearance trials exist.

summary: A stable vitamin A ester used in foods and some skincare; no appearance trials exist.
note: Excess preformed vitamin A has documented toxicity.
currentQuick:
Retinyl acetate is a retinol ester used for food fortification, supplements and some anti-aging creams.
No published trial has tested it on skin appearance.
How it works: It is converted to retinol in the body, which can then be converted to retinoic acid.
Risks and caveats: As with other vitamin A forms, excess intake can cause hypervitaminosis A. Cosmetic concentrations are capped by EU regulators.
deepLead:
Retinyl acetate (vitamin A acetate) is a synthetic, fat-soluble ester of retinol. It is used to fortify foods such as margarine, plant-based milks and cereals, appears in multivitamins, and is included in some anti-aging skincare products, where it is presented as a more stable, gentler alternative to retinol .
After ingestion it is hydrolyzed in the intestine to retinol, which is re-esterified and stored mainly as retinyl palmitate in the liver . No published human trial of topical retinyl acetate for appearance was found.

name: Ceramide EOP

angle.text: Ceramide EOP is a barrier lipid listed in repair moisturisers, used to keep skin hydrated and calm so it looks smoother. Ceramides generally are well studied for barrier function; little is published on this subtype specifically.

summary: A skin-barrier ceramide listed in moisturisers; little is published on this subtype specifically.
note: Subtype-specific evidence is sparse; research is mostly on ceramides as a class.
currentQuick:
Ceramide EOP is one of the skin's own ceramides, which are lipids that help hold water in the outer skin layer. It shows up in barrier-repair moisturisers.
Published material on this particular subtype is thin, so most of what is known comes from ceramides as a group.
How it works: Ceramides sit in the lipid matrix between skin cells with cholesterol and fatty acids, forming a barrier that limits water loss.
Risks and caveats: It is a cosmetic ingredient. No subtype-specific safety or efficacy findings were located.
deepLead:
Ceramide EOP is a skin ceramide, a waxy lipid made of a sphingoid base joined to a fatty acid, that appears on ingredient lists of barrier-repair moisturisers. Ceramides in general are a component of the stratum corneum lipid matrix, where, together with cholesterol and free fatty acids, they form the water-limiting barrier of the outer skin .
The wiki's source base for this specific ceramide subtype is very thin. General encyclopedia coverage of ceramides describes their role in the skin barrier and their inclusion in creams, soaps and some eczema-related topical products, but does not discuss ceramide EOP by name or summarise clinical trials of moisturiser efficacy .

name: Hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid

angle.text: Hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid is hyaluronic acid cut into shorter chains and marketed for deeper hydration and a plumper look. Users apply it in serums; direct evidence for the low-weight form's effect on appearance is thin.

summary: Chopped-up hyaluronic acid sold as the deeper-penetrating hydrator; direct evidence is thin.
note: No standalone topical trials; very small HA fragments have shown pro-inflammatory activity in cell studies.
currentQuick:
Hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid is hyaluronic acid broken into shorter chains. Brands market it as getting deeper into skin than regular HA.
The only human data found come from a multi-ingredient serum, so its own effect has not been isolated.
How it works: HA binds water and supports skin hydration; shorter chains are argued to reach further, though encyclopedia coverage does not address topical penetration.
Risks and caveats: A patch test of a serum containing it reported no irritation or allergy in 55 adults. Laboratory work shows small HA fragments can provoke inflammatory responses in cells.
deepLead:
Hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid is hyaluronic acid (HA) that has been broken into shorter chains, and it is marketed in skincare as a low-molecular-weight form intended for deeper hydration. HA itself is a glycosaminoglycan found in skin and other connective tissues, where it supports hydration .
Encyclopedia coverage of HA notes that chain length matters biologically: high-molecular-weight HA and low-molecular-weight fragments behave differently in cell studies, and some very small fragments have been reported to promote angiogenesis and inflammatory responses . That coverage does not address how well topically applied hydrolyzed HA penetrates skin .
Published clinical evidence specific to hydrolyzed HA as a topical ingredient is limited to a small number of studies of multi-ingredient products.

name: Sodium hyaluronate

angle.text: Sodium hyaluronate is the salt form of hyaluronic acid found in most moisturisers and serums, used for a hydrated, dewy, plumper-looking skin surface. It is well established in medical products; direct data on topical looks effects are limited.

summary: The salt form of hyaluronic acid in most moisturisers and serums; well established medically, with little direct data on topical looks effects.
note: Strong evidence base is for injections and surgery, not facial creams.
currentQuick:
Sodium hyaluronate is the common salt form of hyaluronic acid, a water-binding molecule naturally present in skin and joints. It appears in many moisturisers and serums.
Most clinical research concerns joint injections and eye surgery rather than cosmetic creams.
How it works: It is a humectant that binds water; lower-molecular-weight versions are marketed as penetrating deeper.
Risks and caveats: Topical use is generally described as well tolerated. Injectable forms (fillers) carry reported risks such as bruising, vascular occlusion and granulomas.
deepLead:
Sodium hyaluronate is the sodium salt of hyaluronic acid (HA), a linear polysaccharide of repeating glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine units found in skin, joint fluid and the eye . It is the form usually listed in moisturisers and serums, and it is also used in medical products such as joint injections and ophthalmic surgical viscoelastics.
In skincare it is described as a humectant that binds water; lower-molecular-weight versions are marketed as penetrating deeper . Evidence cited for sodium hyaluronate in the medical literature comes mainly from injectable or surgical uses rather than cosmetic topicals.
